Many scholars say Peter saw the start of Joel's prophecy at Pentecost, with the cosmic signs still to come at the end. Some note the darkness at the crucifixion (Luke 23:44-45) as a partial fulfilment. Futurists keep the sky signs for the future day of the Lord.
Isn't reading the sun, moon and stars as nations just "spiritualizing" the Bible?
The fulfilled reading says no. It reads the Bible as the Bible reads itself. Taking a figure of speech as a figure is the literal sense.

Many believers are taught to read the Bible "literally". The fulfilled reading agrees, if literal means the sense the author meant. Every reader accepts figures of speech. Jesus called himself a door and a vine (John 10:9; 15:1). The trees clap their hands (Isaiah 55:12). The question is how the Bible uses a given image. The nineteenth-century scholar Milton Terry said it takes more than an assertion to prove that Isaiah's figurative language becomes literal when Jesus or Paul uses it. On this reading, the method is the same throughout Matthew 24. We look to the Old Testament to explain each verse. There is no reason to stop when we reach the sun and moon. This is not allegory. It is reading the text in its own language.
Isaiah 55:12: "all the trees of the field shall clap their hands" — a figure no one takes literally.
Milton Terry's Biblical Hermeneutics (1890) argued that the apocalyptic style of the prophets carries into the New Testament.

Dispensationalists hold to "literal, grammatical-historical" reading and accept figures of speech. They argue that the fulfilled view applies figures too widely, to texts that may be literal. They also say that figurative readings of fulfilled prophecy can open the door to reading away clear promises, such as those to Israel.
Is prophecy written in secret codes that only modern readers can crack?
The fulfilled reading says no. Jesus explained himself from Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms. The Old Testament is the key, not hidden codes.

Books such as The Bible Code (1997) claimed that hidden letter patterns in the Hebrew text predict modern events. Popular prophecy writing often acts as if Revelation is an encrypted message that only our generation can read. The fulfilled reading points to Luke 24. After his resurrection, Jesus began "with Moses and all the Prophets" and explained what the Scriptures said about him (Luke 24:27, 44). The disciples' hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures (Luke 24:32). Jesus' first hearers had only the Old Testament. When he spoke of a dark sun and falling stars, they would recognise the words of Isaiah, Ezekiel and Joel. On this reading, the Old Testament is our dictionary for prophecy, and there are no secret codes.
The Bible Code's methods were tested and the same "predictions" were found in Moby-Dick (Brendan McKay, 1997).
Luke 24:44: everything written in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms about Christ had to be fulfilled.

Most scholars of all views reject "Bible code" methods. Futurists agree that the Old Testament is the key to prophecy. They argue that it is the Old Testament promises that point to a future Israel and a future tribulation. Some say parts of Daniel were sealed until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9).
Does the Bible also use bright sun, moon and stars as a picture of blessing?
Yes. When God heals his people, the prophets say the moon will shine like the sun and the sun seven times brighter. This is clearly figurative.

Isaiah 30:26 says that on the day the Lord binds up his people's wounds, the moon will shine like the sun and the sun will be seven times brighter. Taken literally, this would scorch the earth. The verse itself gives the meaning: God "binds up the brokenness of his people". Isaiah 60:19-20 says the sun will no longer set and the moon will not wane, because the Lord will be an everlasting light. Revelation 21:23 uses the same picture for the new Jerusalem. The fulfilled reading sees a pair. Bright lights picture a nation raised up and blessed. Darkened lights picture a nation brought down in judgment. Both are figures for what God does to peoples in history.
Isaiah 30:26: the sun shines seven times brighter "in the day when the Lord binds up" his people.
Isaiah 60:20: "your sun shall no more go down" — followed by "the days of your mourning shall end".

Most scholars agree these blessing texts are figurative. Futurists often place them in a future millennium or the new creation, and some expect real changes in the natural world then. Amillennial scholars usually read them as pictures of the church or the new creation.
If Israel's "lights" went out in AD 70, who now carries God's light to the nations?
On the fulfilled reading, the new covenant people of God—Jews and Gentiles in Christ—carry the light that Israel was called to show the nations.

Israel was called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). On the fulfilled reading, the old covenant order with its temple and priesthood ended in AD 70. Hebrews says God was shaking what can be shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain (Hebrews 12:26-28). It calls the old covenant "ready to vanish" (Hebrews 8:13). Daniel foretold a kingdom that would never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44). Jesus called his disciples "the light of the world" (Matthew 5:14). Peter applied Israel's titles to the church: a chosen people and a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). The first church was made up of Jews, and it then welcomed Gentiles. This reading does not say God has cast off the Jewish people (Romans 11:1-2). It says the light now shines through Messiah's people.
Acts 13:47: Paul and Barnabas apply Isaiah 49:6, "a light for the Gentiles", to their own mission.
Philippians 2:15: believers "shine as lights in the world".

Dispensationalists hold that God's promises to national Israel remain in force and will be fulfilled in a future kingdom. They reject any idea that the church has replaced Israel. Many other scholars hold that Romans 11:25-26 promises a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ.
Can Christians today point to signs that show Jesus will return in our lifetime?
On the fulfilled reading, no. The Olivet signs led up to AD 70. Scripture gives no puzzle of modern signs that dates the final coming.

Read in its setting, the sign list of Matthew 24, Mark 13 and Luke 21 answers the disciples' question about the temple (Matthew 24:1-3). Those signs were wars, famines, false messiahs, persecution and armies around Jerusalem. They came before and during the Roman war of AD 66-70. So this reading holds that the discourse gives no countdown for our day. Jesus said plainly that no one knows the day of the final coming (Acts 1:7). Every generation that has tried to fit current news into a sign puzzle has been wrong. Statements such as "the Antichrist is alive now" or "I will see the rapture in my lifetime" go beyond what the text says. Christians should be ready at all times, not because the news looks dark, but because Christ is Lord and judge at every moment.
A Special Notice in an Oklahoma newspaper on 25 July 1986 said Christ was coming soon and added side predictions about the U.S. President in Jerusalem on 15 May 1988. None of it happened.
In 1991 John Walvoord told Newsweek he expected the rapture in his own lifetime. He died in 2002.

Futurists answer that the signs of Matthew 24 will be repeated or completed in a final tribulation, so the "birth pains" can grow stronger before Christ comes. Historicists see signs spread across church history. Many teachers in all camps agree that no date can be set.
Can the Bible words "soon" and "near" mean an open-ended span of time?
This reading says no. If prophecy is read plainly, "near" must mean near for the people first addressed, not near for some later age.

The New Testament repeatedly told first readers that the Lord's coming was close. James wrote that the coming of the Lord "is at hand" (James 5:8). Peter wrote that the end of all things was near (1 Peter 4:7). Revelation says its events "must shortly come to pass" (Revelation 1:1). On the fulfilled reading, these words had a real meaning for the churches that read them first. A teacher who claims to read prophecy literally cannot turn "near" into "possible at any moment, even after two thousand years." That move, this reading argues, empties the words of their meaning. Instead, the near coming refers to Christ's judgment on Jerusalem within that generation. The final coming at the resurrection is real, but the Bible does not attach these nearness words to a far-future date.
Compare Matthew 26:18: "My time is at hand" meant Jesus' death within days.
Compare Mark 1:15: "The kingdom of God is at hand" meant the kingdom was arriving in Jesus' ministry, not millennia later.

Futurists say "near" means "next on God's calendar" or "imminent," so it could happen at any time. Others appeal to 2 Peter 3:8, that a day is like a thousand years with the Lord, and say God measures nearness differently from people.
If the Olivet signs are past, what does Scripture say must happen before the final return of Christ?
Christ reigns now from heaven until every enemy is put under his feet. When that reign has done its work, he returns to raise the dead and judge.

Paul says Christ must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet; the last enemy is death (1 Corinthians 15:24-26). Psalm 110:1 gives the pattern. The Messiah sits at God's right hand until his enemies become his footstool. Peter quotes this psalm at Pentecost and applies it to the risen Jesus (Acts 2:34-35). Heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool (Isaiah 66:1). So, on this reading, the one "sign" before the end is the completed spread of Christ's rule. This is not a calendar sign. It is a process. When the reign has finished its work, the dead are raised and the living and dead are judged. The text sets no date, and it calls for faithful work, not anxious watching of headlines.
Psalm 110:1 is the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New Testament, applied to Jesus' present reign in Acts 2, Hebrews 1 and 10.
Hebrews 10:12-13 pictures Christ seated, "waiting" until his enemies are made a footstool.

Premillennialists agree Christ reigns now in heaven, but hold that the defeat of enemies will be finished in a future earthly kingdom after his return. Amillennialists agree with a present reign but expect evil to grow until the end. Postmillennialists expect wide gospel success before he comes.
Does 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 teach a secret rapture followed later by an earthly millennium?
This reading says no. The text speaks of resurrection, meeting the Lord, and being with him for ever. It says nothing of a later seven years or an earthly kingdom.

Paul comforts grieving believers. The Lord comes with a shout and a trumpet; the dead in Christ rise first; the living are caught up with them; and so they are with the Lord always (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). On this reading, the passage describes one public event: the resurrection at the last day. Nothing in it mentions a tribulation before or after, a return seven years later, a rebuilt temple, or a restored sacrificial system. The verse ends with "for ever with the Lord." No further stage is named. The two-stage scheme must therefore be brought to the text from other passages. This reading holds that this is reading in, not reading out. The plain point is hope at death and resurrection.
The shout, the archangel's voice and the trumpet are loud and public, not secret (compare 1 Corinthians 15:52).
Jesus links resurrection to "the last day" in John 6:39-40, not to a day seven years before the end.

Pretribulationists say the passage describes the Lord coming for his church, while other texts describe his coming with his saints later. They argue the church is not appointed to wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9). Posttribulationists agree the event is single and public but place it after a future tribulation.
Which event does Matthew 24:30, the Son of Man coming on the clouds, describe?
On the fulfilled reading, it describes Christ's vindication and his judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, because Jesus put it within "this generation."

Jesus said that all these things would happen before that generation passed away (Matthew 24:34). The coming on the clouds stands inside "all these things." It also follows "immediately after" the tribulation of those days (Matthew 24:29). So this reading concludes that verse 30 cannot be a rapture or the final bodily return far in the future. It is the moment when Jesus is shown to be the enthroned Son of Man, and his rule is displayed in judgment on the city that rejected him. The wording comes from Daniel 7:13, where the Son of Man receives a kingdom. The destruction of the temple was public proof that the old order had ended and that Jesus had been given authority.
Matthew 16:27-28 also ties the Son of Man coming "in his kingdom" to some who were standing there.
The temple burned in August of AD 70 (the month of Av), within about forty years of the prophecy (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-6.4.8).

Futurists read verse 30 as the visible Second Coming after a future tribulation. Some preterists and many evangelical scholars split the discourse, applying the near signs to AD 70 and the cloud-coming to the end. Others see a double fulfillment: AD 70 as a preview of the final coming.
Why does Matthew 24 give so much detail about the tribulation but say nothing of a rapture, rebuilt temple or earthly millennium after Jesus comes?
This reading says the silence is because those events are not in the prophecy. The discourse is about the fall of the old temple, not a later kingdom program.

Jesus gave careful detail about the time before the city fell: when to flee, not to go back for a coat, to pray it would not be winter (Matthew 24:16-20). If a rapture and a thousand-year kingdom followed straight after his coming, one would expect at least a word about them. Yet verse 30 is followed by the gathering of the elect and the parable of the fig tree. There is no rebuilt temple, no new Israeli state and no earthly reign from Jerusalem. On the fulfilled reading, the silence is meaningful. The subject is the end of the old covenant age and the passing of its temple. Any later program must be supplied from outside the passage.
Compare the precise instruction in Luke 21:20-21: when you see armies around Jerusalem, flee to the mountains.
Church tradition records that Jerusalem Christians left for Pella before the siege (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3).

Dispensationalists answer that Matthew 24 focuses on Israel's tribulation, while the rapture is revealed later to the church in Paul's letters, and the kingdom details come from Revelation 20 and the Old Testament prophets. Silence, they say, is not denial.
When the prophets say God "comes down" in judgment, as in Micah 1:3-4, is that a visible, bodily coming?
No. In Micah God "came" against Samaria and Jerusalem through the Assyrian and Babylonian armies. Nobody saw God himself, and the mountains did not literally melt.

Micah says the Lord comes out of his place, treads on the heights, and the mountains melt like wax (Micah 1:3-4). The target is named: Samaria and Jerusalem (Micah 1:5). Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC. In neither case did people see God walking on the hills. The language is poetic. It means God acted in history to judge. On this reading, the New Testament uses the same kind of language for Christ's coming against Jerusalem in AD 70. The words are no less true for being figurative. They tell us who stands behind the armies of history: God himself.
Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6).
Isaiah 19:1 says the Lord rides a swift cloud into Egypt; the judgment came through human rulers (Isaiah 19:2-4).

Many futurists agree that Old Testament "comings" were figurative, but argue that Jesus' coming is unique because he has a human body and ascended visibly (Acts 1:11). So, they say, his return must also be visible and bodily.
What do clouds stand for when the Bible links them with God?
Clouds mark God's presence, glory, rule and judgment. They are a sign of the divine King at work, not a weather report.

God led Israel in a pillar of cloud (Exodus 13:21). He came to Sinai in a thick cloud (Exodus 19:9). Cloud filled the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10-12). Clouds and darkness surround his throne (Psalms 97:2). He makes the clouds his chariot (Psalms 104:3). The day of the Lord is a day of clouds (Ezekiel 30:3; Joel 2:2). Clouds are the dust of his feet (Nahum 1:3). Across these texts the cloud is a symbol of divine presence, often in judgment. So when the Son of Man "comes with clouds," a Jewish listener would hear a claim to divine authority, the right to act as God acts. On the fulfilled reading, that is the point of Matthew 24:30.
The cloud at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:5) marks God's presence and voice.
Nahum 1:3 used cloud language for God's judgment on Nineveh, which fell in 612 BC.

Interpreters of all schools accept that clouds signal divine glory. Futurists add that Acts 1:9-11 shows Jesus left in a literal cloud and will return "in the same way," so the cloud imagery at the final coming is also literal.
Is God riding a swift cloud into Egypt (Isaiah 19:1) meant literally?
No. The picture shows God ruling over nations. Egypt's judgment came through civil war and a harsh ruler, not a visible God on a cloud.

Isaiah pictures the Lord riding a fast cloud into Egypt. The idols tremble and Egyptians fight one another (Isaiah 19:1-2). God then gives them over to a cruel master (Isaiah 19:4). The events are political and military. No Egyptian saw God sitting on a cloud. In the same way, Psalm 104 says God walks on the wings of the wind and makes the winds his messengers (Psalms 104:3-4). No one takes this as physical description. The question this reading asks is simple: if this language is figurative in the Old Testament, why should the same language suddenly be read with wooden literalism when Jesus uses it about Jerusalem? Consistency asks that Scripture be read by its own patterns of speech.
Egypt was conquered by Assyria under Esarhaddon in 671 BC; many see this as the fulfillment of Isaiah 19:4.
Psalm 18:9-11 describes God bending the heavens and coming down in darkness to rescue David from Saul.

Futurists agree Isaiah 19:1 is figurative, but they argue that the New Testament adds literal details to Jesus' return, such as a visible body, a shout, and the gathering of believers. Those details, they say, mark it off from Old Testament imagery.
In Daniel 7:13, which way does the Son of Man travel: down to earth or up to God?
Up. He comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and is presented before him to receive a kingdom.

Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. He comes to the Ancient of Days, is brought near before him, and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). The movement is toward God's throne, not toward the earth. The aim is not to collect saints but to receive royal power. On this reading, when Jesus quotes this verse (Matthew 24:30; 26:64), he is speaking of his enthronement, which took place at his resurrection and ascension. AD 70 then publicly showed that this enthronement was real. Scholars such as R. T. France and N. T. Wright argue that the Daniel text speaks of vindication and exaltation, not descent.
Acts 1:9 and Mark 16:19: Jesus is taken up in a cloud and sits at God's right hand, matching Daniel's direction of travel.
Ephesians 1:20-22: God seated Christ far above all rule and put all things under his feet.

Many futurist and traditional scholars accept that Daniel 7:13 shows an ascent, but argue that the New Testament reuses the phrase for Christ's return (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16), so its direction can be reversed in later fulfillment.
What did Jesus mean when he told the high priest, "From now on you will see the Son of Man... coming on the clouds" (Matthew 26:64)?
On this reading, Caiaphas would witness the evidence that Jesus had been raised and enthroned: the rise of the church and the judgment that fell on the temple leaders.

Jesus spoke to Caiaphas and the council, using "you." He said that from now on they would see him seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds (Matthew 26:64). "From now on" points to the near future, not to a time thousands of years later. Caiaphas did not need to see a figure flying in the sky. He would see events that proved Jesus right: the empty tomb reports, the growth of the apostles' movement, and finally the collapse of the temple system that had condemned him. On this reading, these events vindicated Jesus as a true prophet and as the Messiah who reigns from heaven.
Luke 22:69 reads "from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God."
Acts 4:5-13: the same rulers face the apostles and cannot deny that a healing miracle has happened in Jesus' name.

Futurists say "you will see" means the judges will see Jesus when they stand before him at the final judgment after their resurrection. Others say "from now on" refers to the enthronement only, while the cloud-coming is still future.
Why did the high priest tear his robes and call Jesus' words blasphemy?
Because Jesus claimed to be Daniel's Son of Man who shares God's throne. The high priest understood it as a claim to divine rule.

When Jesus joined Psalm 110:1 (seated at God's right hand) with Daniel 7:13 (coming with the clouds), he claimed the highest place beside God. Caiaphas tore his robes and said Jesus had blasphemed (Matthew 26:65). This shows that the high priest heard a claim about authority and throne, not a claim about a far-off trip through the sky. On this reading, Jesus was saying that he would occupy David's throne in heaven (Acts 2:30-36). God raised him and seated him over every power (Ephesians 1:20-23). So the temple and its priesthood had become obsolete. In a sense, the high priest grasped the meaning of Daniel 7 better than many modern date-setters.
Matthew 22:41-46: Jesus earlier used Psalm 110:1 to ask how David's son can also be David's Lord.
Leviticus 21:10 forbade the high priest to tear his clothes in mourning; his act showed extreme outrage.

All Christian views agree that Jesus claimed divine authority here. Futurists add that his claim will be finally displayed at his visible return, when every eye sees him. Some also see the cloud-coming in Jesus' reply as still future for Caiaphas, to be seen at the last judgment.
What did Stephen see in Acts 7:56, and why does it matter for the meaning of the Son of Man's "coming"?
Stephen saw Jesus standing at God's right hand. On this reading, he saw the enthroned Son of Man and announced judgment on those who rejected him.

Just before his death Stephen said he saw heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand (Acts 7:56). This is the only time outside the Gospels that the title "Son of Man" is used by a human speaker. It matches Daniel 7: the Son of Man before God's throne. Stephen had just charged his hearers with resisting the Holy Spirit and killing the prophets (Acts 7:51-52). On this reading, the vision confirmed that the kingdom had passed to Jesus and his people (Matthew 21:43). The sentence on the temple leaders would be carried out within a generation. Stephen, like his Lord, prayed for the forgiveness of his killers (Acts 7:60).
Matthew 21:43: the kingdom will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruit.
1 Peter 2:9 calls the church, made of believing Jews and later Gentiles, a "holy nation."

Many interpreters see Stephen's vision as Jesus rising to welcome his martyr or to act as his advocate. They do not tie it to AD 70, and futurists still expect a later bodily coming of the Son of Man.
Is "the sign of the Son of Man in heaven" a visible object in the sky?
On this reading, no. The sign is that the Son of Man is in heaven, enthroned. The fall of the temple was the proof of it.

The Greek of Matthew 24:30 can be read word for word: "then will appear the sign of the Son of Man in heaven." The word ouranos means heaven as well as sky. The phrase "in heaven" belongs most naturally with "the Son of Man," not with "the sign." So the sign shows that the Son of Man is in heaven, ruling. On this reading, the visible event was on earth: the end of the temple and city. That event proved that Jesus sat at the Father's right hand (Acts 2:33; Hebrews 9:24). Some early writers expected a visible sign, such as a cross in the sky, but even they did not think the sign was Jesus himself.
Matthew 12:39-40: the only sign given to that generation was the sign of Jonah, that is, Jesus' resurrection.
Josephus reports strange portents before the war, but these are reports, not the meaning of Jesus' sign (Jewish War 6.5.3).

Futurists expect a visible sign in the sky at the Second Coming. Early writers such as the Didache (16:6) spoke of a sign spread out in heaven, and some have suggested the Shekinah glory or a great cross. Others take the sign to be Christ himself appearing.
Does "all the tribes of the earth will mourn" in Matthew 24:30 mean every people on the planet?
On this reading, it means "all the tribes of the land," that is, Israel in Judea. The Greek word ge often means land.

The Greek word ge can mean soil, ground, the land of Israel, or the whole earth. Context decides. In Matthew 2:20-21 it clearly means the land of Israel. In the Olivet Discourse Jesus is speaking to Jews about Judea (Matthew 24:16). "Tribes" is a natural word for Israel's twelve tribes. Zechariah 12:10-14, which lies behind this verse, describes the families of the land of Israel mourning, clan by clan. Some translators, such as Ronald Knox, render it "the tribes of the land." The Hebrew word eretz behaves the same way: it often means the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). On this reading, the mourning belongs to first-century Judea, not to all nations.
Luke 21:23 speaks of "great distress in the land and wrath upon this people," using the same word.
Zechariah 12:12-14 lists the mourning by family: David, Nathan, Levi, Shimei.

Most translations and futurist interpreters read "all the tribes of the earth," linking it with Revelation 1:7 and the worldwide reach of the final return. Some see a first fulfillment in Israel and a fuller one among all nations.
Who are "those who pierced him" in Zechariah 12:10 and Revelation 1:7, and when did they see him?
On this reading, they are first-century Judeans connected with the crucifixion, who "saw" him in the judgment of AD 70 within their generation.

Zechariah 12:10 says people of Jerusalem will look on the one they pierced and mourn. The order of Zechariah's Messiah prophecies is telling. The king on a donkey (9:9) was fulfilled at the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:5). The thirty pieces of silver and the potter (11:12-13) were fulfilled with Judas (Matthew 27:3-10). The struck shepherd and scattered sheep (13:7) were fulfilled at Jesus' arrest (Matthew 26:31). The piercing and mourning stand between these first-century events. John 19:37 applies the piercing to the crucifixion. So Revelation 1:7, written to people expecting things "soon," fits the generation that crucified him. It is important to add that the New Testament blames the leaders and the crowd of that day. It never blames Jewish people as a whole for all time. Many Jews mourned and believed (Acts 2:37-41).
Acts 2:36-37: listeners were "cut to the heart" when told they had crucified the Lord.
Matthew 27:3-10 fulfills the thirty-pieces-of-silver prophecy of Zechariah 11:12-13.

Futurists see Zechariah 12:10 fulfilled when Israel as a nation turns to Jesus at his return, linking it with Romans 11:26. Revelation 1:7 is then read as worldwide sight of the returning Christ. Some see both an AD 70 and a final fulfillment.
How could people "see" the Son of Man coming if he did not appear bodily in the sky?
In Scripture, "seeing" often means understanding. The crucifiers would grasp, through the judgment, who Jesus really was.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:10: God blinded their eyes so they would not see, understand and turn (John 12:40). This blindness is spiritual, not physical. In Luke 24:31 the disciples' eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus. Paul was sent to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light (Acts 26:18). Romans 15:21 says those who were not told will "see," that is, understand. On this reading, "every eye will see him" means people would perceive his power at work as he judged the city and prospered his church. They did not see his body after the ascension, but they saw his rule in their history. The Greek verb horao (future opsontai) can mean perceive as well as look.
John 3:36: whoever does not obey the Son "will not see life," meaning will not experience it.
Luke 17:22: the disciples will long "to see" one of the days of the Son of Man.

Futurists answer that "every eye" in Revelation 1:7 is universal and physical, as Acts 1:11 promises Jesus will come back "in the same way" he left. They grant that "see" can mean understand, but say this context requires literal sight.
After AD 70, where is the centre of God's worship and the throne of David?
In heaven. Christ sits on David's throne in the heavenly Jerusalem, and worship is no longer tied to one mountain or city.

Jesus told the Samaritan woman that an hour was coming when people would worship the Father neither on her mountain nor in Jerusalem (John 4:21-24). He called his own body the temple (John 2:19-21). Peter preached that God swore to seat David's descendant on his throne, and that this happened when Jesus was raised and exalted to God's right hand (Acts 2:30-33). Paul calls believers children of "the Jerusalem above" (Galatians 4:26). Hebrews says Christians have come to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). On this reading, the fall of the earthly temple confirmed this change. The promises of a son of David on the throne for ever are fulfilled in Jesus now.
